What's the difference between margin and padding?

Padding is space inside an element, between its content and its border (the background shows through it). Margin is space outside the border, separating the element from its neighbours (it is transparent). Vertical margins between block siblings can collapse into the larger of the two; padding never collapses.

CSS specificity - why is my class being ignored? ```css #nav a { color: grey; } .link { color: red; } ``` ```html
Home
```

Specificity decides, not order. `#nav a` has an id (1,0,0) plus an element (0,0,1), while `.link` has only a class (0,1,0), so the grey rule wins. Fix it by lowering the first selector's specificity, for example `nav a`, or by matching it: `#nav .link { color: red; }`. Avoid `!important`; it makes later overrides harder.
When should I use grid and when flexbox?

Use flexbox for one-dimensional layouts: a row of buttons, a navbar, items distributed along a line. Use grid for two-dimensional layouts where rows and columns must line up, like a page layout or a card gallery. They combine well: a grid for the page, flexbox inside each card.

```css
.gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; }
```

Is it fine to use a div with an onClick as a button?

It's better to use `<button type="button">`. A `div` isn't focusable, doesn't react to Enter or Space, and has no button role for screen readers; you would have to add `tabindex`, `role="button"` and key handlers yourself. A native button gives all of that for free, and you can restyle it fully with CSS.
What should alt text say?

Describe the image's purpose in context, briefly. A product photo: "Red running shoe, side view". A chart: say the main takeaway, with data in text nearby. Purely decorative images get an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip them. Don't start with "image of", and don't leave out the attribute entirely.
What's the point of semantic HTML tags?

Tags like `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<section>`, `<footer>` and `<button>` tell browsers, assistive technology and search engines what each part is. Screen-reader users can jump between landmarks, keyboard behaviour comes built in, and your CSS and tests get clearer hooks than a sea of `<div>`s.
Why does my page look zoomed out on phones?

Without a viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop width (about 980px) and scale it down. Add this to `<head>`:

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

Then make sure your CSS uses flexible widths rather than fixed pixel widths.
defer vs async on script tags?

Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing. `defer` runs scripts after the document is parsed, in the order they appear, which suits most app code. `async` runs each script as soon as it arrives, in any order, which suits independent scripts like analytics. Scripts without either block parsing while they download and execute.
Why doesn't `z-index` work on my element?

`z-index` only affects positioned elements (anything except `position: static`), flex or grid items, and it only competes within its stacking context. If a parent creates its own stacking context (via `position` with `z-index`, `transform`, `opacity < 1`, `filter` and similar), a child can never rise above elements outside that parent, no matter how large its z-index. Inspect the ancestors, and give the element `position: relative` if it has none.
How do I truncate long text with an ellipsis?

For one line:

```css
.title { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }
```

For multiple lines, use the line-clamp pattern, which is widely supported:

```css
.excerpt { display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 3; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; overflow: hidden; }
```

In a flex child you may also need `min-width: 0`.
Light/dark mode with CSS only?
This button's hover style doesn't show on touch devices. Is that a bug?

It's expected: touch screens have no real hover, and many browsers emulate it with a sticky state after a tap. Don't hide important information behind `:hover`. Use `@media (hover: hover)` to apply hover-only styling on devices that support it, and give `:focus-visible` and `:active` states as well.
What does `box-sizing: border-box` do?

By default (`content-box`) the `width` you set covers only the content, so padding and borders make the element wider. With `border-box`, the width includes padding and border, which makes layout arithmetic predictable. Most projects set it globally:

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```

That's a stale closure. The effect ran once, so the callback captured `count` from the first render and never sees later values. Options:

1. Put `count` in the dependency array so the interval is recreated when it changes (fine for logging).
2. Keep the latest value in a ref: `const latest = useRef(count); latest.current = count;` and read `latest.current` inside the interval.
3. If you only update state, use the updater form (`setCount(c => c + 1)`) so no captured value is needed.

The `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule flags exactly this mistake.
What should go in the useEffect dependency array?

Every reactive value (props, state, and variables derived from them) that the effect reads. React compares them between renders and re-runs the effect when one changes. An empty array means "run once after mount", which is only correct if the effect truly uses no reactive values. Don't silence the lint rule; instead restructure: move functions inside the effect, use `useCallback` for stable callbacks, or use the updater form of `setState`. Objects and arrays created inline in the component are new on every render, so depending on them re-runs the effect each time.
React warns 'Each child in a list should have a unique key'. What is it and what should I use?

Keys let React match list items between renders, so it can reorder, insert and remove items correctly and keep their state. Use a stable unique identifier from your data, such as a database id:

```jsx
{todos.map(t => <TodoItem key={t.id} todo={t} />)}
```

Avoid the array index if the list can be reordered, filtered or inserted into: items then keep the wrong state (like input text). Never generate keys with `Math.random()` during render, because they change every time and force remounting.
How do controlled inputs work in React?
Two sibling components need the same data. Where does the state go?
When should I use React.memo, useMemo and useCallback?

Not by default. React re-rendering is usually cheap. Reach for them when you have measured a problem (the Profiler shows slow renders), typically:

- `React.memo` on a component that is expensive to render and often receives the same props.
- `useMemo` for an expensive calculation, or to keep an object/array prop referentially stable for a memoised child.
- `useCallback` for a function passed to a memoised child or used in an effect's dependencies.

Memoisation has its own cost and adds complexity. Often it is better to move state down, or split a component, so fewer things re-render.

Yes. React detects changes by comparing references; `push` mutates the same array and `setTodos(todos)` passes the same reference, so React may skip the re-render, and memoised children won't update. Create a new array:

```jsx
setTodos(prev => [...prev, t]);
```

Same for objects: `setUser(u => ({ ...u, name }))`. Treat state as read-only.
useState vs useReducer - which should I use?
Can I call hooks inside an if statement?
How do I write a custom hook, e.g. for a debounced value?
When do I need a ref instead of state?

Use a ref for values that must persist across renders but whose change shouldn't cause a re-render: DOM nodes (`ref={inputRef}`), timer ids, the previous value, or a mutable instance variable. Use state for anything the UI displays. Don't read or write `ref.current` during rendering for display logic; do it in event handlers and effects.
How do I submit a form without a page reload in React?
Is dangerouslySetInnerHTML really dangerous?

It bypasses React's automatic escaping, so any user-controlled HTML can run script in your page (XSS). Prefer rendering text normally with `{value}`, which React escapes. If you must render user-supplied HTML (for example Markdown output), sanitise it with a well-maintained sanitiser such as DOMPurify before inserting it, and add a Content-Security-Policy as a second layer.
How should I structure a growing React project?

Organise by feature rather than by file type: a folder per feature (`orders/`, `auth/`) containing its components, hooks, API calls and tests, plus a small `shared/` for generic UI. Keep components focused, move data fetching into hooks or a query library, and avoid prop drilling by lifting state sensibly or using context for truly global concerns (theme, current user). Enforce boundaries with lint rules so features don't import each other's internals.
How should I test a React component?
What is the difference between props and state?

Props are inputs passed into a component by its parent; the component treats them as read-only. State is data the component owns and can change over time, with a setter that triggers a re-render. A good rule: if a value can be computed from props or other state, don't store it in state; compute it during render.
What is context good for, and when is it a bad idea?

Context passes values through the tree without threading props, which suits things many components read and rarely change: theme, locale, the signed-in user. Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes, so it is a poor fit for rapidly changing data (such as input text or mouse position) or a large state object that many components use for different parts. Split contexts by concern, memoise the provider value, or use a state library with selectors when updates are frequent.
Why is my useEffect running twice in development?

In React's Strict Mode (the default in many dev setups), React deliberately mounts, unmounts and remounts components in development to expose effects that lack proper cleanup. It doesn't happen in production builds. The fix is not to disable Strict Mode but to make the effect resilient: return a cleanup function that undoes the setup (cancel the request, close the connection, clear the timer) so a second run is harmless.
My list of 10,000 rows is slow. What do I do?

Rendering thousands of DOM nodes is the bottleneck. Options, in order of impact: virtualise the list so only visible rows are in the DOM (react-window or TanStack Virtual); paginate or filter on the server; keep row components cheap and memoised with stable keys; avoid creating new inline objects or functions per row. Measure with the browser's performance panel and the React Profiler before and after.
How do I share state across routes after login?

Keep the authenticated user in a top-level provider (context) or a small store, populated when the app loads (for example by calling a session endpoint) and updated after login or logout. Protect routes with a wrapper component that redirects when there is no user. Remember this only controls the UI: the server must still enforce authorisation on every request, since a user can change client code.

How do I validate a JSON request body in FastAPI?
What does Depends do in FastAPI?
Should my FastAPI route be async def or def?

Use `async def` when the function awaits non-blocking I/O (an async database driver, `httpx.AsyncClient`). Use plain `def` when it calls blocking code (a synchronous database library, `requests`, heavy file I/O): FastAPI runs those in a thread pool so they don't block the event loop. The worst combination is `async def` that calls blocking code, which freezes every request while it runs. If you must do CPU-heavy work, move it to a worker process.

I get a CORS error calling my FastAPI backend from the browser. How do I fix it?

`Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/api' from origin 'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy`

The browser blocks cross-origin requests unless the server says they're allowed. Add the CORS middleware with the exact origins you trust:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["http://localhost:5173"],
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
    allow_credentials=True,
)
```

Don't combine `allow_origins=["*"]` with credentials; browsers reject it and it would be unsafe anyway. In development you can alternatively proxy API calls through your frontend dev server so the browser sees one origin. CORS is a browser protection, not authentication.
Which HTTP status codes should my API return for create, validation errors, not found and unauthorized?

Common choices:

- 201 Created for a successful POST that creates a resource (with a `Location` header if you can).
- 200 OK for reads and updates; 204 No Content for a successful delete with no body.
- 400 for a malformed request; 422 for a well-formed request with invalid data (FastAPI's default for validation).
- 401 when the caller isn't authenticated, 403 when they are but aren't allowed.
- 404 when the resource doesn't exist (or you don't want to reveal that it does).
- 409 for conflicts such as a duplicate unique value.
- 429 when rate limited, and 5xx only for server faults.

In FastAPI: `raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Task not found")`.
How should I check a bearer token in FastAPI?

Use a dependency so every protected route shares the same check:

```python
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer

bearer = HTTPBearer()

def current_user(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(bearer)):
    user = verify_token(creds.credentials)   # your function: check signature, expiry, audience
    if user is None:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, "Invalid token", headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    return user
```

Verify the signature with a fixed expected algorithm, check expiry, issuer and audience, and keep the signing key in configuration, not in code. Authentication (who you are) is separate from authorisation (what you may touch), so also check ownership inside each route.
My FastAPI endpoint returns the SQLAlchemy object with the password hash in it. How do I prevent that?
How do I test FastAPI endpoints?

Use `TestClient` with pytest; it calls your app in-process without starting a server:

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app

client = TestClient(app)

def test_create_task_validates_title():
    r = client.post("/tasks", json={"title": ""})
    assert r.status_code == 422

def test_create_task():
    r = client.post("/tasks", json={"title": "Write docs"})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    assert r.json()["title"] == "Write docs"
```

Override dependencies (database, current user) in tests so they are fast and isolated.

Review this FastAPI code:

```python
@app.get("/search")
async def search(q: str):
    rows = db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{q}%'").fetchall()
    return rows
```

Problems:

1. **SQL injection**: `q` is formatted straight into the SQL. Use bound parameters.
2. **Blocking call in `async def`**: a synchronous driver blocks the event loop; use `def` or an async driver.
3. **Unbounded output**: no limit or pagination.
4. **`SELECT *`** may expose columns you didn't intend.

```python
from sqlalchemy import text

@app.get("/search")
def search(q: str = Query(min_length=1, max_length=50), limit: int = Query(20, le=100)):
    stmt = text("SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE :pat LIMIT :lim")
    rows = db.execute(stmt, {"pat": f"%{q}%", "lim": limit}).mappings().all()
    return rows
```

(`Query` comes from `fastapi`.) Escape `%` and `_` in `q` if literal matching matters.
Where should I put business logic in a FastAPI app?

Keep route functions thin: parse and validate the request, call a service function, translate the result into a response. Put the rules in plain Python modules (services) that don't import FastAPI, and put queries in a repository or data layer. That makes the logic easy to unit-test without HTTP and lets other entry points (CLI jobs, workers) reuse it.
How do I run something after the response in FastAPI, like sending an email?
How do I load configuration (database URL, secret key) in a FastAPI project?

Read settings from environment variables once at startup into a typed settings object, instead of hard-coding them:

```python
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    secret_key: str
    debug: bool = False

settings = Settings()
```

`pydantic-settings` is a separate package in Pydantic v2. Missing required values fail fast at startup. Keep real secrets out of the repository (use a `.env` file listed in `.gitignore`, or your platform's secret store), and never log them.
How do I handle errors in an Express app?
What is middleware in Express?

Middleware is a function `(req, res, next)` that runs in order for matching requests. It can read or change the request and response, end the response, or call `next()` to pass control on. Typical uses: logging, JSON body parsing (`express.json()`), authentication, rate limiting and error handling. Order matters: a middleware that needs a parsed body must be registered after the parser.
Why does `await` in my Express route not stop the server from serving other requests?

Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, but `await` on I/O (database, network, file) yields control, so other requests are handled meanwhile. What does block everyone is long synchronous work: `JSON.parse` on huge inputs, `fs.readFileSync`, crypto in a tight loop, a big `for` loop. Move CPU-heavy work to a worker thread or another process, and prefer the async versions of APIs.
How do I validate request input in a Node API?
How should I store a user's password in a Node app?

Never store plain text or fast hashes like SHA-256. Use a slow, salted password hashing algorithm such as bcrypt or argon2 through a maintained library:

```javascript
const bcrypt = require('bcrypt');
const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);        // store this
const ok = await bcrypt.compare(attempt, hash);       // on login
```

The library generates the salt and embeds it in the hash. Enforce a sensible minimum length, rate-limit login attempts, and respond with the same message for unknown user and wrong password so you don't leak which accounts exist.
What's the best way to structure a Node API project?

A common, practical layout separates concerns into layers: routes (HTTP only), controllers or handlers (parse input, call services, shape the response), services (business rules), and data access (queries). Configuration is loaded once from the environment, and the app creation is separate from `listen()` so tests can import the app without starting a server. Keep modules small and avoid circular imports. The exact folder names matter less than keeping HTTP details out of business logic.
Is it okay to use `process.env.SECRET` directly throughout the code?
My Node server crashes with 'Unhandled promise rejection'. What does it mean?

A promise was rejected (an async function threw, or `reject` was called) and nothing handled it with `catch` or `try/catch`. Since Node 15 this terminates the process by default. Fix the root cause: add `try/catch` around awaited calls, or `.catch()`, and make sure every promise is either awaited or has a handler. As a last-resort safety net you can log in `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)`, but a crashing process after a logged error and a restart by a supervisor is usually safer than limping on in an unknown state.
How do I rate limit an API?

Count requests per client (IP, API key or user) in a time window and respond with 429 and a `Retry-After` header when the limit is exceeded. In Express, middleware such as `express-rate-limit` does this for a single instance. If you run multiple instances, the counters must live in shared storage (like Redis), or a gateway or CDN must enforce the limit. Apply stricter limits to sensitive endpoints such as login and password reset.
How should I design pagination for a list endpoint?

Two common patterns:

- **Offset/limit** (`?page=3&per_page=20`): simple and lets users jump to a page, but slow on large offsets and unstable if rows are inserted between requests.
- **Cursor/keyset** (`?after=<last_id>&limit=20`): the server returns the next cursor; it stays fast on large tables and is stable under inserts.

Whichever you choose, cap the maximum page size, use a deterministic sort order (add a tie-breaker such as `id`), and return pagination info:

```json
{"items": [], "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDQyfQ"}
```
What does idempotent mean for an API, and which methods should be?

An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE` are meant to be idempotent; `POST` is not by default, so a retried request can create duplicates. For operations like payments, accept an `Idempotency-Key` header: store the key with the result and, if the same key arrives again, return the saved response instead of repeating the work. This makes client retries after timeouts safe.
What should an API error response look like?
How should I version my API?

Pick one scheme and apply it consistently: a path prefix (`/v1/users`) is the simplest and most visible; headers or media types are cleaner in theory but harder to use and cache. Only bump the version for breaking changes; adding optional fields or new endpoints is backward compatible. Announce deprecations with a date and a `Deprecation`/`Sunset` header where you can, and keep the old version running until clients have migrated.
PUT or PATCH for updating a resource?

`PUT` replaces the whole resource with the representation you send (missing fields are cleared or defaulted), and is idempotent. `PATCH` applies a partial change (only the fields sent). For most UI-driven updates, `PATCH` matches what clients want. Whatever you choose, validate which fields may be changed, and never let clients update fields like `id`, `role` or `owner_id` by passing them in the body.
Should I use plural or singular nouns in REST URLs, and what about actions?

Use plural nouns for collections (`/orders`, `/orders/42`) and let the HTTP method express the action: `GET /orders`, `POST /orders`, `DELETE /orders/42`. For operations that aren't plain CRUD, either model them as a sub-resource (`POST /orders/42/cancellation`) or a clearly named action endpoint (`POST /orders/42/cancel`). Consistency matters more than purity.
How do I make an endpoint safe for concurrent edits (two users editing the same record)?

Use optimistic concurrency. Include a version number or `ETag` with each record; the client sends it back with its update (`If-Match` header or a `version` field). The server applies the update only if the version still matches, using something like `UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :version`. If no row was updated, return 409 (or 412) so the client can reload and merge. Pessimistic locks are an alternative for short critical sections but hurt throughput.
When would GraphQL make sense instead of REST?

GraphQL fits when many different clients need different shapes of the same data (a mobile app wants less than a web app) and you want to avoid over-fetching and many round trips. The costs: query complexity and N+1 problems need careful control, caching is harder than with plain HTTP, and authorisation must be enforced per field. For a simple CRUD API with one client, REST is usually simpler.
What's a good way to handle file uploads in an API?

Validate size, type and count on the server, never trusting the client's file name or `Content-Type`. Store files outside the web root or in object storage with generated names, serve them with a safe `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition`, and scan if the content is risky. For large files, let clients upload directly to object storage with a short-lived signed URL so your API server isn't a bottleneck.
What's the difference between `interface` and `type` in TypeScript?

For object shapes they are largely interchangeable. `interface` can be extended and merged (declaration merging: two interfaces with the same name combine), which suits public library APIs. `type` can also name unions, intersections, tuples and mapped types, which an interface can't do. A practical rule: use `interface` for object contracts, `type` for everything else, and be consistent within a codebase.
What does `as` do, and when is it a bad idea?

`as` is a type assertion: you tell the compiler to treat a value as a given type. It does no runtime check. It's reasonable when you know more than the compiler (for example, narrowing a DOM element to `HTMLInputElement`). It's dangerous for external data such as `JSON.parse(x) as User`, where nothing guarantees the shape. Validate the data (hand-written guard or a schema library) and let the validator produce the type instead.
Explain generics with a practical example.
Utility types - which ones should I know?

The most useful: `Partial<T>` (all fields optional), `Required<T>`, `Readonly<T>`, `Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'>` (keep some fields), `Omit<T, 'password'>` (drop fields), `Record<K, V>` (object with given key and value types), `ReturnType<typeof fn>`, and `NonNullable<T>`. Example: `type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>;` keeps the types in sync as `User` evolves.
How do I type a function that can return different shapes depending on input?
Why do I get 'Type string is not assignable to type "a" | "b"'?

A string literal union only accepts those exact literals. A variable declared with `let x = 'a'` is widened to `string`, which doesn't fit. Fix it by annotating the type (`let x: 'a' | 'b' = 'a'`), using `const x = 'a'` (which keeps the literal type), or `as const` on objects: `const opts = { mode: 'a' } as const;`.
Should I turn on `strict` in tsconfig for an existing project?

Yes, ideally, but migrate gradually. `strict` enables `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny` and several related checks that catch real bugs. On a large codebase, turn the flags on one at a time (or per-folder with project references), fix the errors in each step, and avoid blanket `any` or `@ts-ignore` to make the errors go away. New code can be strict from day one.
What is XSS and how do I prevent it?

Cross-site scripting happens when an attacker's text ends up in your page as executable HTML or script, for example a comment containing `<script>`. Prevent it by escaping output for the context it's placed in (modern frameworks do this by default for text), avoiding `innerHTML`/`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with untrusted data, sanitising any HTML you must allow with a vetted library, and adding a Content-Security-Policy. Also mark session cookies `HttpOnly` so injected script can't read them.
What's CSRF and do I need protection if I use JWTs?

CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request to your site, relying on cookies being attached automatically. If authentication is by a cookie (session or JWT in a cookie), you need protection: `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` cookies, plus CSRF tokens for state-changing requests where appropriate. If the token is sent explicitly in an `Authorization` header by your own JavaScript, browsers don't attach it automatically, so classic CSRF doesn't apply, but then the token is reachable by script, which makes XSS more serious.
Is it safe to store a JWT in localStorage?

It's a trade-off. Anything in `localStorage` can be read by any script running on the page, so an XSS bug lets an attacker steal the token. An `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie can't be read by script, but then you need CSRF defences. Many teams use short-lived access tokens kept in memory plus a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie. Whatever you pick, keep tokens short-lived, and make XSS prevention a priority.
What are common JWT mistakes?

Typical ones: accepting the algorithm named in the token header (always specify the allowed algorithm on verification, and reject `none`); not checking expiry, issuer or audience; putting sensitive data in the payload (it is only encoded, not encrypted); using a weak or hard-coded signing secret; making tokens long-lived with no way to revoke them; and using a JWT where a simple server-side session would be easier and safer.
How do I prevent SQL injection in code?

Never build SQL by concatenating or formatting user input. Use parameterised queries or your ORM's bound parameters, so the driver sends the SQL and the values separately:

```python
cur.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))
```

Parameters protect values, not identifiers: for dynamic table or column names, check them against an allow-list. Also give the application's database account only the privileges it needs.
What's wrong with committing a .env file?

It puts secrets (API keys, database passwords, signing keys) into version control history, where anyone with repo access, including future contributors and forks, can read them, and deleting the file later doesn't remove it from history. Add `.env` to `.gitignore`, commit a `.env.example` with placeholder names, and load real values from your host's secret store. If a secret was ever committed, treat it as compromised: rotate it.
How do I handle user-uploaded images safely?

Check the actual content, not just the extension: verify the file type with a library, limit the size and dimensions, and re-encode images (which strips embedded payloads and metadata). Store them under random names outside the web root or in object storage, serve from a separate domain or with `Content-Disposition` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and never execute or include uploaded files. SVG can contain script, so treat it as active content.
What is a Content-Security-Policy?

A CSP is a response header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images and other resources are allowed. For example `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` blocks inline scripts and scripts from other origins, which greatly limits what an XSS bug can do. Roll it out in report-only mode first to find what breaks, avoid `'unsafe-inline'`, and use nonces or hashes for scripts you must inline.
Should I validate input on the client, the server, or both?

Both, for different reasons. Client-side validation is for user experience: quick feedback. It's not a security control, since anyone can bypass the browser and send raw requests. Server-side validation is mandatory: check types, ranges, lengths, allowed values and ownership every time. Share the rules (schemas) between client and server where your stack allows it, so they don't drift.
How do I store API keys in a frontend app?

You can't keep a secret in code that ships to the browser; anyone can read it from the bundle or network tab. Keys that must stay secret belong on your server: the frontend calls your backend, which calls the third-party API. Public keys designed for client use (such as a map tile key) should be restricted by domain and quota in the provider's settings.
What does `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` on a cookie do?

`HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript (limits theft via XSS). `Secure` sends it only over HTTPS. `SameSite=Lax` stops the browser from sending it on most cross-site requests (reducing CSRF) while still allowing top-level navigations such as clicking a link. A session cookie should normally have all three, plus a sensible expiry.
Explain the principle of least privilege in code and infrastructure.

Give every user, service and process only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. For an app: a database account that can't drop tables, an API token scoped to read-only if it only reads, containers that don't run as root, and role checks on each endpoint. If something is compromised, the damage is limited to what that component could do.
Monolith or microservices for a new product with a team of five?

Start with a modular monolith. One deployable unit is simpler to build, test, debug and run, and with clear module boundaries you can extract a service later if a real need appears (independent scaling, different release cadence, a separate team). Microservices bring network failures, distributed transactions, versioned contracts and heavy operational tooling, which a five-person team usually can't afford early on.
What problem does a cache solve and what are the risks?

A cache stores the result of expensive work (a query, a computation, a remote call) so repeated requests are fast. The risks are stale data, inconsistent data across instances, and cache stampedes when a popular key expires and many requests rebuild it at once. Decide how stale is acceptable, set a TTL, invalidate on writes where correctness matters, and add jitter or a lock for hot keys. Measure the hit rate; a cache with a low hit rate only adds complexity.
When should I use a message queue?

Use a queue when work doesn't need to finish within the request: sending emails, generating reports, resizing images, calling slow third parties. The web process enqueues a job and returns quickly, and workers process it with retries and rate control. Queues also smooth traffic spikes and decouple components. Remember the cost: at-least-once delivery means jobs can run twice, so make handlers idempotent, and add a dead-letter path for jobs that keep failing.
What is a layered architecture, and what's the benefit?

Layers separate responsibilities: presentation (HTTP/UI), application or service logic, domain rules, and data access. Dependencies point one way (top to bottom), so business rules never import web framework code and can be tested without a server or database. The benefit is changeability: you can swap the database or add a CLI without rewriting the rules. The risk is over-layering a small app, where it adds files without adding clarity.
What does 'stateless' mean for a web service and why does it matter?

A stateless service keeps no per-user data in its own memory between requests; everything needed arrives with the request or lives in shared storage (database, cache). Then any instance can serve any request, so you can add or remove instances, restart them or deploy without losing sessions, and a load balancer can distribute traffic freely. Keep sessions in a shared store or in signed tokens instead of process memory.
Explain eventual consistency in plain language.

After a write, different parts of the system may briefly show different values, but if no new writes occur they all converge to the same value. A social feed that shows your new post to followers a second or two later is an example. It is the price of availability and scale in distributed systems. It is fine for likes and feeds, but not for something like a bank balance, which needs stronger guarantees.
How do I decide between SQL and NoSQL for a new project?

Start from your data and queries. Relational databases suit structured data with relationships, transactions and ad-hoc queries, and are the right default for most applications. Document or key-value stores suit flexible schemas, very high write throughput, or simple access by key, at the cost of weaker joins and cross-record transactions. Many systems use both: a relational database as the system of record plus a cache or search index. Choosing NoSQL only because it "scales" is rarely the best reason.
What is a circuit breaker in a service?

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency. After enough failures or timeouts it "opens" and fails fast for a while instead of waiting on a broken service, then lets a few trial requests through to test recovery. This prevents one slow dependency from tying up all your threads and cascading the outage. Pair it with timeouts, retries with backoff, and a sensible fallback or degraded response.
Why shouldn't I let the frontend talk to the database directly?

The database credentials would have to live in code the user controls, and any user could run arbitrary queries. A backend sits between them to authenticate users, authorise each action, validate input, enforce business rules and limit what is exposed. Some managed platforms do offer direct access, but only with row-level security rules enforced on the database side, which must be designed and tested carefully.
How do I design for observability?

Emit three kinds of signals: structured logs (JSON with a request id), metrics (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, queue depth) and traces that follow a request across services. Propagate a correlation id through every call, log at meaningful levels without secrets or personal data, and alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency) rather than only on causes (CPU). Add health endpoints for liveness and readiness.
What's the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication answers "who are you?": verifying identity with a password, token or key. Authorization answers "what may you do?": checking permissions for a specific action on a specific resource. Passing authentication doesn't imply permission. A frequent bug is checking only that a user is logged in and not that the requested record belongs to them (an insecure direct object reference).
I want to add background jobs to a small app. Do I need Kafka?

Almost certainly not. Kafka is a distributed log designed for high-volume event streaming, and it is operationally heavy. For ordinary background jobs, a simple queue backed by your existing database or Redis (or a managed queue) with a worker library is far simpler. Consider Kafka when you need replayable event streams, many independent consumers, or very high throughput.
What are feature flags and why use them?

A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns a feature on or off without redeploying. Teams use them to merge unfinished work safely, roll out to a percentage of users, run experiments, and disable a misbehaving feature instantly. The cost is extra code paths and test combinations, so remove flags once a rollout is complete.
How should I handle database migrations safely in production?

Make each migration small and reversible when possible, version them in source control and run them in CI against a copy of the schema. Use the expand/contract pattern for breaking changes: add the new column (nullable), deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column in a later release. Avoid long table locks (add indexes concurrently where supported) and take a backup first.
What should I unit test and what should I leave to integration tests?

Unit-test pure logic and decision-heavy code (calculations, parsing, validation, state transitions), where inputs and outputs are clear and tests are fast. Use integration tests for the seams: your code with a real database, HTTP routes with serialisation and middleware, and external-service adapters (with the service faked at the network edge). A few end-to-end tests cover the most critical user journeys. Many cheap tests at the bottom, fewer slow ones at the top.
My tests pass locally but fail in CI. Where do I start?

Look for differences between environments: dependency versions (pin them with a lockfile), environment variables, time zone and locale, file paths and case-sensitivity, and the order of tests. Then flaky causes: shared state between tests, reliance on test order, real network calls, timing (`sleep`) and random data without a seed. Re-run the failing test in isolation and in a fresh clone, read the first failure rather than the last, and make tests independent.
What is mocking and when does it go wrong?

A mock replaces a collaborator (a clock, an HTTP client, a payment gateway) with a controllable stand-in so a test is fast and deterministic. It goes wrong when the mock encodes assumptions that are no longer true, so tests pass while the real integration is broken, or when tests assert on how code calls its dependencies rather than on observable results. Mock at system boundaries, prefer fakes for things you own, and keep a few integration tests against the real thing.
How many assertions should a test have?

There's no fixed number; a test should check one behaviour. Several assertions are fine when they describe different facets of one outcome (status code and body of one response). If a test needs a paragraph to describe or fails for unrelated reasons, split it. Name tests after the behaviour (`test_rejects_negative_quantity`), so a failure message tells you what broke.
What does 'test coverage' tell me and what doesn't it?

Coverage tells you which lines or branches ran during tests. It can reveal untested code, but it can't tell you whether the tests check anything: a test with no assertions still counts. High coverage with weak assertions gives false confidence. Use it to find gaps, aim for meaningful coverage on critical paths, and prefer techniques like mutation testing or code review of the assertions when quality matters.
Explain test-driven development briefly. Is it worth it?

TDD means: write a failing test for the next small behaviour, write the simplest code to pass it, then refactor with the tests as a safety net. It yields small, testable designs and a regression suite as a by-product. It is most valuable for logic-heavy code with clear inputs and outputs, and less natural for exploratory UI work. You don't have to follow it dogmatically; writing tests just after the code but in small steps captures much of the benefit.
What's a good branching strategy for a small team?

Trunk-based development with short-lived branches works well: branch from `main`, keep changes small, open a pull request, run CI, review and merge within a day or two, and deploy from `main`. Use feature flags for unfinished work instead of long-running branches. Long-lived branches diverge and produce painful merges. Protect `main` so it requires passing checks and a review.
I committed a secret to Git and pushed. What do I do?

First, treat the secret as compromised and rotate it immediately (revoke the old key, issue a new one); removing it from the repo does not undo the exposure. Then remove it from the code and load it from the environment. Optionally rewrite history with a tool such as `git filter-repo` and force-push, but coordinate with collaborators, and remember forks and clones may still hold the old commits. Add secret scanning in CI to catch it next time.
What makes a good commit message?

A short imperative summary line (about 50 characters) saying what the commit does, a blank line, then a body explaining why the change was needed and anything non-obvious, wrapped at about 72 columns. Example: `Fix off-by-one in pagination` followed by a sentence describing the symptom and cause. Keep each commit to one logical change so it can be reviewed, reverted or cherry-picked on its own.
I accidentally committed to main instead of a feature branch. How do I fix it (not pushed yet)?

Create the branch at your current commit, then move `main` back:

```bash
git branch feature/my-change        # keeps the commit on a new branch
git reset --hard origin/main         # main goes back to the remote's state
git switch feature/my-change
```

The `reset --hard` discards uncommitted changes in your working tree, so make sure nothing else is uncommitted. If you have already pushed `main`, don't reset: use `git revert` instead.
What's the difference between `git fetch`, `git pull` and `git clone`?

`git clone` copies a whole repository for the first time. `git fetch` downloads new commits and branches from the remote into your remote-tracking branches without touching your working files. `git pull` is `fetch` plus an integration step (merge by default, or rebase if configured) into your current branch. Fetch first when you want to look before you merge.
My pull request has merge conflicts. What's the cleanest way to resolve it?

Update your branch with the target branch and resolve conflicts locally:

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main      # or: git merge origin/main
# edit conflicted files, then:
git add <files>
git rebase --continue
```

Rebase gives a linear history but rewrites your commits, so you need `git push --force-with-lease` afterwards; use it only on your own branch. Merge is safer if others share the branch. After resolving, rerun the tests, since a clean textual merge can still be a logical conflict.
What does `git stash` do and when would I use it?

It saves your uncommitted changes onto a stack and restores a clean working tree, so you can switch branches or pull quickly, then bring the changes back with `git stash pop`. It's handy for context switches, such as an urgent bug fix. Use `git stash push -m "message"` to label entries, `git stash list` to see them, and avoid leaving stashes around for weeks, since they are easy to forget.
How do code reviews work best?

Keep pull requests small (ideally a few hundred lines) and describe the why, how to test, and anything risky. Reviewers should check correctness, edge cases, tests, readability and security, ask questions rather than issue orders, and separate must-fix from nice-to-have comments. Automate the mechanical things (formatting, linting, tests) so humans can focus on design and logic. Respond to feedback promptly in both directions.
My React app shows a blank page after I deployed it to a subfolder (example.com/app/). It worked locally.

That pattern usually means asset paths are wrong. Open the browser's developer tools: in the Network tab, are the JavaScript files returning 404 (probably requesting `/assets/...` from the domain root)? And does the Console show errors?
yes, the js files 404. they're requested from /assets/index.js

Then your build assumes it's served from `/`. Tell the bundler the base path. With Vite, set `base: '/app/'` in `vite.config.js` and rebuild; with Create React App, set `homepage` in `package.json`. If you use client-side routing, also configure the router's basename (for React Router: `<BrowserRouter basename="/app">`), and make the server fall back to `index.html` for unknown paths under `/app/` so refreshing a deep link doesn't 404.
now the page loads but refreshing /app/settings gives 404

That's the server-side fallback. Static hosts only serve files that exist, so `/app/settings` isn't found. Configure a rewrite to `index.html`: in nginx, `location /app/ { try_files $uri /app/index.html; }`; on many static hosts there's a setting such as 'single-page app' or a rewrite rule file. The router then reads the URL and renders the right screen.
My API is slow, around 3 seconds per request. Where do I start?

Measure before guessing. Break the request time into parts: network, application code, database, external calls. Do you have logging, a profiler or APM, or can you at least time the main steps? And is it slow for every endpoint or just one?
just the /orders list endpoint. it loads orders and their items

That sounds like an N+1 query problem: one query for the orders, then one query per order for its items. Enable query logging and count the SQL statements per request. If you see hundreds, load the items in bulk with a join or an `IN (...)` query (with an ORM, use eager loading such as `selectinload` or `joinedload`). Also check that the foreign key column `order_id` is indexed.
yes 240 queries. I added eager loading and it's 4 queries now, but still 800ms

Good progress. Now look at those four: run `EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) on each and look for full table scans or large sorts. Check whether you return more data than the page needs (select only the needed columns, paginate). If the numbers are still large, a covering index for the filter and sort columns, or caching the result for a short time, is the next step.
Python: my script prints 'ModuleNotFoundError: No module named requests' even though I installed it.

That usually means you installed it into a different Python than the one running the script. Run `python -m pip show requests` and `python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"` with the same interpreter. Are you using a virtual environment?
I have two pythons. pip installs to 3.9 but I run python3.12

Install with the interpreter you run, so they always match: `python3.12 -m pip install requests`. Better, create a virtual environment for the project (`python3.12 -m venv .venv`, activate it, then `pip install -r requirements.txt`) so dependencies stay isolated and `python` and `pip` refer to the same environment.
git push says 'rejected - non-fast-forward'. What now?

It means the remote branch has commits you don't have locally, so Git won't overwrite them. Run `git fetch` and look at `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/<branch>` to see what's there. Is this a shared branch or just yours?
shared with a teammate. they pushed this morning

Then integrate their work first: `git pull --rebase` (or `git pull` for a merge) to put your commits on top of theirs, resolve any conflicts, run the tests, and push again. Don't use `--force` on a shared branch, since it would delete your teammate's commits from the remote.
My Docker container exits immediately after starting.

Check why: `docker logs <container>` shows its output, and `docker ps -a` shows the exit code. A container stops when its main process ends or crashes. What does the Dockerfile run (`CMD` or `ENTRYPOINT`)?
CMD ["python", "app.py"] and the log says 'No such file or directory: app.py'

The file isn't where the container expects. Make sure it is copied in and that the working directory is right:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . /app
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

Also check `.dockerignore` isn't excluding it, and that the build context contains `app.py`. You can look inside with `docker run --rm -it <image> sh` and `ls`.
Why is `fetch('/api/data')` returning HTML instead of JSON in my SPA?

A request for `/api/data` is receiving your app's `index.html`, which means the request isn't reaching the API. Common causes: the dev server has no proxy configured for `/api`, the production server's SPA fallback rule catches `/api` too, or the API runs on another port or host. Check the Network tab for the response and which server answered. Which setup are you using in development?
Vite dev server, API on port 8000
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map') in my React component. I'm doing `data.items.map(...)`.

`data.items` is `undefined` at the moment of the render. Typically the data hasn't loaded yet (initial state is `null` or `{}`), or the API response has a different shape than you expect. Do you initialise `data`, and what does the response look like?
useState(null) and then I fetch. the response is {"results": [...]}
My cron job runs fine manually but not from cron.

The usual cause is the environment: cron runs with a minimal `PATH`, no shell profile, a different working directory and no virtualenv. Use absolute paths for the interpreter and script, set the working directory, and capture output so you can see the error: `* * * * * cd /srv/app && /srv/app/.venv/bin/python job.py >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1`. Does anything in your script depend on environment variables?
yes, it needs DATABASE_URL

Cron doesn't load your shell's variables. Define it in the crontab (`DATABASE_URL=...` at the top), source an env file in the command (`set -a; . /etc/app.env; set +a;`), or have the script read the settings file itself. Keep the secret file readable only by the job's user.
I changed my CSS but the browser still shows the old styles.

That's almost always caching. Try a hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R) or open the dev tools Network tab with 'Disable cache' ticked. If it persists, check that the file you edited is the one actually loaded (view the source of the stylesheet in the Sources tab), that the build step ran, and whether a service worker is serving an old copy. Is this local or a deployed site?
deployed behind a CDN

Then the CDN is serving a cached copy. Best practice is to fingerprint filenames at build time (`app.3f2a1c.css`) so every change gets a new URL and you can cache forever; HTML should have a short cache time or revalidate. As a quick fix, purge the file in the CDN.
Why does `npm install` give me peer dependency errors?

A package you're installing declares that it needs a specific version range of another package (a peer dependency), and your project has a version outside that range. Read the message: it names the package, the required range and what you have. Which packages does it mention?
react 19 but a library wants react ^18

Check whether the library has a newer release that supports React 19; upgrading it is the clean fix. If not, you can stay on React 18 until it does. `--legacy-peer-deps` or `--force` will bypass the check, but that can leave you with a library that breaks at runtime, so use it only knowingly and test the app.

It prints `10,20,30`. Each `setTimeout` is scheduled with its own delay, so the callbacks fire in order of delay (10, 20, 30), not in the order they were created. The last timer (50 ms) fires after all of them and prints the collected values.

Awaiting one after the other runs them sequentially, so the time is the sum of both. `Promise.all` starts both before waiting, so the time is the longer one. The check prints:

```
sequential takes about the sum: true | parallel takes about the max: true
```

Use `Promise.all` for independent operations, but keep sequential awaits when the second depends on the first.

Use the built-in `URL` and `URLSearchParams` instead of splitting strings by hand; they handle decoding (`+` becomes a space) and repeated keys. Output:

```
node js
2
[ 'a', 'b' ]
```

Remember that every value is a string, so convert and validate numbers, and use `getAll` for keys that can repeat.

Store each value with an expiry timestamp and check it on read, deleting expired entries lazily. Output:

```
1
undefined
```

This is fine for one process. It has no size limit (add an eviction policy such as LRU for real use), and with several server instances each has its own copy, so use a shared cache like Redis when consistency matters.

`async` doesn't make code run in the background; it only lets `await` yield. A synchronous loop runs to completion on the single thread, so the 10 ms timer cannot fire while it spins. Output:

```
ticks during busy loop: 0
ticks after yielding: true
```

Once the code awaits, the event loop gets control back and the timer runs. For CPU-heavy work use a worker thread or a separate process.

Ignore the client's file name for storage: generate a random name and keep only an allow-listed extension. That removes path traversal (`../../`), odd characters and collisions. Output:

```
true
type not allowed
```

Keep the original name in the database if you want to show it to the user, and check the file's content type as well.
whats the difference between GET and POST

GET asks for a resource and should have no side effects; its parameters travel in the URL, so it can be cached, bookmarked and repeated safely. POST sends data in the request body to create something or trigger an action, and is not cached or repeated automatically. Never put secrets in a GET URL, since URLs are logged by servers and proxies.
Explain what happens when I type a URL into the browser.

In outline: the browser checks its caches, resolves the domain name to an IP address through DNS, opens a TCP connection (and a TLS handshake for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, and the server responds with HTML. The browser parses the HTML, fetches linked CSS, JavaScript and images (each possibly a new request), builds the DOM and render tree, runs scripts, and paints the page. Each step has caching and optimisation opportunities, such as CDNs, keep-alive connections and HTTP/2.
Why do I get 'Mixed Content' warnings?

Your page is loaded over HTTPS but requests a resource (script, image, API) over plain HTTP. Browsers block or warn about this because an attacker could tamper with the insecure resource. Fix it by using `https://` URLs (or protocol-relative paths) for every resource and API call, and make sure your server redirects HTTP to HTTPS.
What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies?

`localStorage` keeps strings per origin until cleared, about 5 MB, and is not sent to the server. `sessionStorage` is the same but lasts only for the tab session. Cookies are small (about 4 KB), can be sent with every request to the server, can have an expiry and flags like `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite`. Use cookies for server sessions, the web storage APIs for non-sensitive client preferences, and none of them for secrets that script shouldn't read.
What does a 304 status mean?

Not Modified. The browser sent a conditional request (with `If-None-Match` and an `ETag`, or `If-Modified-Since`), and the server says the cached copy is still valid, so it sends no body. It saves bandwidth while keeping content fresh.
What is a CDN and when do I need one?

A content delivery network caches copies of your static files (and sometimes pages) on servers close to users, which reduces latency and load on your origin. It's valuable when you have users spread over regions, large assets or traffic spikes. For a small site with a local audience, a CDN isn't essential, though many hosts include one anyway.
What is the difference between a framework and a library?

You call a library: it provides functions you use where you decide. A framework calls you: it defines the structure and flow, and you plug your code into it (routes, components, handlers). Frameworks give conventions and speed but make you work their way; libraries are more flexible but leave more decisions to you.
Why does my fetch not send cookies to the API?

By default `fetch` doesn't include credentials for cross-origin requests. Set `credentials: 'include'` on the request, and on the server respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and a specific allowed origin (not `*`). For same-origin requests `credentials: 'same-origin'` (the default) is enough. Cookies with `SameSite=Strict` or `Lax` may also be withheld on cross-site requests.
What is the DOM?

The Document Object Model is the browser's in-memory tree of objects representing your HTML page. JavaScript uses it to read and change the page: `document.querySelector('#title').textContent = 'Hi'`. Changing the DOM triggers layout and painting, so batch updates and avoid reading layout properties in the middle of writing them in a loop.
How does the browser decide when to use a cached file?

Through HTTP caching headers. `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` lets the browser reuse a file without asking for a year, which is ideal for fingerprinted assets. `Cache-Control: no-cache` means "revalidate before using", typically with an `ETag`. Use long caching with hashed file names for JS/CSS/images, and short or revalidated caching for HTML so users get new versions.
My `position: sticky` header doesn't stick.

Sticky positioning needs three things: a `top` (or other offset) value, no ancestor with `overflow: hidden`, `auto` or `scroll` between the element and the scrolling container (those make that ancestor the scroll context), and enough room in its parent, since it only sticks within the parent's box. Check the ancestors in dev tools for `overflow` and for a parent that is only as tall as the header itself.
Why is there a gap under my image?

Images are inline elements by default and sit on the text baseline, which leaves space for descenders below them. Set `img { display: block; }` or `vertical-align: top`. Also check there is no line-height or font-size on the container creating extra space.
What does `rem` vs `em` vs `px` mean?

`px` is a fixed CSS pixel. `rem` is relative to the root element's font size (usually 16px), so it scales with the user's browser setting and gives consistent spacing. `em` is relative to the current element's font size, which compounds when nested. Use `rem` for most sizing so the layout respects user preferences, `em` for things that should scale with their own text (such as button padding), and `px` for thin borders.
My animation is janky. How can I make it smoother?
How do I stop a Node app from logging my users' emails and tokens?

Treat logs as data that spreads. Log events and ids rather than payloads, redact known sensitive keys (password, token, authorization, cookie) in a central logger wrapper, and never log full request headers or bodies by default. Review error handlers, since exceptions often include the data that triggered them. Set retention limits on log storage and restrict who can read it.
What's the event loop in one paragraph?

Node runs your JavaScript on one thread. When you start asynchronous work (a timer, a network or file operation), Node hands it to the system and keeps going; when it finishes, its callback is queued. The event loop picks queued callbacks and runs them one at a time, with promise callbacks (microtasks) running before the next timer or I/O callback. Long synchronous code delays everything, because nothing else can run until it returns.
What should a good `package.json` scripts section contain?

Short, consistent commands for the workflows people repeat: `dev` (run with reload), `build`, `start` (production), `test`, `lint` and `format`. CI should call the same scripts developers use. Commit the lockfile so installs are reproducible, and pin the Node version with the `engines` field or an `.nvmrc` file.
Flask or FastAPI for a new small API?

Both are fine. FastAPI gives you request validation, automatic OpenAPI documentation and first-class async support through type hints, so it suits JSON APIs. Flask is minimal and flexible, with a huge ecosystem, and works well for server-rendered pages or when you want complete control. If the API's main job is validating and serving JSON, FastAPI usually saves time.
My Python API leaks memory over days. How do I find the cause?

Start by confirming it: graph the process's memory over time. Then look for common causes: unbounded caches or global dictionaries/lists that only grow, objects kept alive by closures or reference cycles with `__del__`, unclosed connections or file handles, and per-request data stored at module level. `tracemalloc` (standard library) can compare snapshots to show which lines allocate memory that isn't freed. As a mitigation, restart workers periodically (for example the max-requests setting in your server), but still fix the root cause.
How do I run tasks on a schedule in a Python web app?

Don't use a sleeping thread inside the web process: with several workers it runs multiple times and dies with the process. Use a separate scheduler (cron, a systemd timer, or your platform's scheduled jobs) to run a command, or a job queue with a scheduler component. Make jobs idempotent and log each run, so a double run or a missed run doesn't cause damage.

Review my Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM python:latest
COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
CMD python app.py
```

It works, but several improvements matter:

- Pin the base image (`python:3.12-slim`) instead of `latest`, so rebuilds are reproducible.
- Copy `requirements.txt` and install before copying the rest, so the dependency layer is cached when only code changes.
- Set a `WORKDIR`, avoid running as root, and add a `.dockerignore` (exclude `.git`, `.env`, caches).
- Use the exec form for `CMD`.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```
pydantic gives me 'Field required' for a field that I think I sent. Why?

The usual causes: the key name doesn't match exactly (case, `userId` vs `user_id`), the value is nested under another key, the client sent the body as form data or with the wrong `Content-Type` so the body wasn't parsed as JSON, or you declared the model as a query parameter. Read the error's `loc` list, which shows where Pydantic looked, and print the raw request body to compare. If you need to accept a different key name, use an alias: `user_id: int = Field(alias='userId')`.
What does `readonly` do in TypeScript and does it freeze the object?

`readonly` prevents assignment to a property or array through that type at compile time. It does not freeze the object at runtime; other code with a non-readonly reference can still change it, and `Object.freeze` is what makes a shallow runtime freeze. Use `readonly` in function parameters to document and enforce that you won't mutate the argument.

How do I undo `git add` for a file I staged by mistake?

`git restore --staged path/to/file` unstages it and keeps your edits in the working tree. On older Git versions, `git reset HEAD path/to/file` does the same. To see the state afterwards, run `git status`.
What is the difference between `git revert` and `git reset`?

`git reset` moves the branch pointer back, discarding commits from the branch history (and with `--hard`, your working changes too), which rewrites history. `git revert` adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, leaving history intact. Revert is the right choice for commits already shared; reset is for local clean-up of work nobody else has.
What does a `.gitignore` do and what should go in it?

It lists patterns of files Git should not track. Typically: dependency folders (`node_modules/`, `.venv/`), build output (`dist/`, `build/`), caches and logs, editor settings, operating-system files and, above all, local secrets such as `.env`. It affects only untracked files, so something already committed must be removed with `git rm --cached` first.

Look at this and tell me what could go wrong in production:

```python
def charge(user_id, amount):
    balance = get_balance(user_id)
    if balance >= amount:
        set_balance(user_id, balance - amount)
        return True
    return False
```

It has a race condition: two concurrent calls can both read the same balance, both pass the check, and both write, so the user is charged less than they should be (or goes negative). Make the check-and-update atomic, for example in one SQL statement inside a transaction:

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amount
WHERE id = :user_id AND balance >= :amount;
```

Then check the affected row count (1 means success). Also use integer cents or `Decimal` for money, validate that `amount` is positive, and make the operation idempotent with a request key so a retry doesn't charge twice.

Accessibility and robustness issues:

- `outline: none` removes the keyboard focus indicator; keep one or replace it with a visible style (for example with `:focus-visible`).
- `#aaa` on `#eee` has very low contrast (well under the 4.5:1 WCAG guideline for normal text).
- 11px text is small, and fixed `width`/`height` break when the text grows or the user increases font size; use padding and `min-height`, with `rem` units.

```css
.btn { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; min-height: 2.5rem; font-size: 1rem; color: #1a1a1a; background: #e6e6e6; }
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #2457d6; outline-offset: 2px; }
```

I wrote this SQL in my API. Opinions?

```python
sql = "UPDATE users SET name = '%s' WHERE id = %s" % (name, user_id)
cur.execute(sql)
```

This is vulnerable to SQL injection: `name` or `user_id` can contain quotes or SQL and change the statement. Never use string formatting for queries. Pass parameters separately:

```python
cur.execute("UPDATE users SET name = %s WHERE id = %s", (name, user_id))
```

The driver quotes the values safely (the `%s` here is the driver's placeholder, not Python formatting). Also check that the current user is allowed to update that `user_id`.
